papers.title_in_file: Non-asymptotic Approximation Error Bounds of Parameterized Quantum Circuits
papers.version_note: arXiv:2310.07528v2 (8 Oct 2024), the NeurIPS 2024 camera-ready; the record id names 2024 and the file name carries the 2023 first version.
papers.what_it_is: A theory paper that constructs data re-uploading PQCs for multivariate polynomials, Lipschitz and Hölder smooth functions, proves non-asymptotic approximation bounds, compares circuit size with ReLU networks, and runs two small simulations.

existing.note: Each bound is for a stated function class and circuit family, not one bound for all PQCs. The Lipschitz bound (via Bernstein polynomials) is in terms of the polynomial degree and the circuit size; the Hölder bound holds only on the union of the localized hypercubes, not on the trifling region; the continuous-function theorem gives existence of a degree with no rate. The Hölder bound is in terms of K, d and the smoothness; width, depth and parameter counts are given separately in each theorem.
existing.value: The paper proves non-asymptotic approximation error bounds for explicitly constructed data re-uploading PQCs: for Lipschitz continuous functions through Bernstein polynomials (a bound in the polynomial degree n, with the circuit width, depth and parameter count given in n), and for Hölder smooth functions through a localized Taylor expansion (a bound in K, d and the smoothness, valid on the union of the localized hypercubes and not on the trifling region, with width, depth and parameter count given in K, d, s and the localization width). The universal-approximation theorem for continuous functions gives only the existence of a degree n, with no rate.

existing.certainty_reason: Theorem 3's bound is printed garbled and its constants differ from Lemma S8; Lemma S9's stated circuit size is smaller than its proof's own count by a factor n; Theorem 4's proof drops a term. Details are in the new assertions.
existing.reader_inference: Reading the proofs, three points need the coordinator's attention: (1) Lemma S9's proof gives depth of order d(n+1)^(d+1) log(n+1) and (n+1)^d times d(n+2) parameters, an extra factor n over the O(d n^d log n) and O(d n^d) that Lemma S9 and Theorems 2 and 3 state; (2) the Theorem 4 proof bounds the PQC output against the Taylor expansion taken at the localization output and then drops that first term (D.64 to D.66) with no argument; (3) the nested circuit builds the basis state from a rounded expectation value of the localization circuit, so it is not a single coherent circuit.

existing.value: The authors state the paper investigates the expressivity of PQCs for approximating multivariate function classes and that they also validate approximation by numerical experiments.
quotes: This paper investigates the expressivity of PQCs for approximating general multivariate function classes.
We further validate the approximation capability of PQCs through numerical experiments.
existing.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of its scope (Abstract).
existing.reader_inference: The numerical experiments (Section 4) train a circuit of the same shape, with the Taylor coefficients held in a separate classical matrix; they are a proof of principle, not a test of the constructed circuits.

existing.note: The paper limits the comparison: it compares the paper's own upper bounds with the upper bounds of Lu et al. for ReLU networks, for smooth-function classes with smoothness index s, 2 <= s < d, treats terms depending only on s as constants, takes d much larger than s, and takes the error as 'some constant'. The 'exponentially smaller' statement is the conclusion drawn from that comparison. Under the stated scalings the size ratio still carries a factor in epsilon (see reader_inference).
existing.value: The authors state that, for the same approximation error, the model size of their PQCs (width times depth) compared with the near-optimal ReLU networks of the cited Lu et al. result has a ratio of the stated scaling order when 2 ≤ s < d, with the approximation error taken as some constant, terms depending only on s treated as constants and d much larger than s; they conclude that the required circuit size and number of parameters of the PQCs is exponentially smaller than the network size and number of parameters of those ReLU networks.
quotes: Remarkably, when 2 ≤ s < d, an intriguing observation emerges: the ratio of model sizes between PQCs and FNNs [21] exhibits a scaling behavior of O(ε−d/(2s)/sd2−d logs d).
when they yield the same approximation error ε (say some constant)
we identify terms that solely rely on the variable s as constants and d ≫ s within Table S1
is exponentially smaller than the required network size and number of parameters of ReLU FNNs
existing.certainty_reason: A comparison of the paper's upper bounds with another paper's upper bounds, drawn under stated simplifications; no lower bound on either side.
existing.reader_inference: From the printed scalings the PQC size is of order K_Q^d with K_Q of order d^2/eps^(1/s), that is eps^(-d/s), and the ReLU size is of order K_C^(d/2), that is eps^(-d/(2s)); the stated ratio therefore contains eps^(-d/(2s)) in its numerator and grows as eps shrinks at fixed d. The ratio is below one only while the s-dependent denominator outweighs it, which holds for eps not exponentially small in d. So the advantage is for large d with eps held constant, not for the limit of small error. The text layer prints the exponents flat; the coordinator should check this reading against the PDF.

assertions.reader_inference: (1) D.64 splits the error into the PQC-versus-Taylor term and the Taylor remainder, then D.65 and D.66 keep only the remainder: the first term is set to zero though the Taylor polynomial is taken at the localization output, not at the exact grid point, and the localization error epsilon is never carried. (2) The proof says the norm of x minus the localization output is at most 1/K, but the coordinatewise bound gives the root of d over K, which is what the theorem's d^(s+beta/2) needs. (3) Section D.4 applies the theorem with s = 0, outside the stated s in the positive integers. (4) The grid index is obtained as the floor of K times an expectation value; this is a classical rounding step inside the 'nested' circuit.

assertions.value: The authors report training a single-qubit PQC to learn the piecewise-constant localization function D(x) on 200 random points in [0, 1], with L = 764 parameters for K = 2 and L = 996 for K = 10, using the Adam optimizer with learning rate 0.01, MSE loss, at most 300 iterations and batch size 100, reaching test MSE 3.57 × 10−4 for K = 2 and 1.04 × 10−4 for K = 10.
quotes: We randomly sample 200 data points within the domain [0, 1] to create training and test datasets for D(x).
A single-qubit PQC with adjustable parameters L = 764 (L = 996) is used to learn D(x) with K = 2 (K = 10).
We use the Adam optimizer [55] with a learning rate of 0.01 to minimize the Mean Squared Error (MSE) loss function during training.
The training process was limited to a maximum of 300 iterations with a batch size of 100 data points.
The achieved MSE on the test data was 3.57 × 10−4 (K = 2) and 1.04 × 10−4 (K = 10).
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.
assertions.reader_inference: This is a trained single-qubit circuit, not the constructed polynomial of Lemma S12. Both test errors are above the 10−4 early-termination level. Run on a classical CPU simulation; the text mentions no noise model and no shot count. The train and test split of the 200 points is not stated.

assertions.value: The authors report approximating a bivariate polynomial on the unit square with a nested PQC of 12 two-qubit PQCs of depth 2, with the Taylor coefficients stored in a separate matrix of size K2 × 12, with 120 trainable parameters for K = 2 and 1272 for K = 10, reaching test MSE 2.22 × 10−4 for K = 2 and 9.82 × 10−5 for K = 10, and state that the approximation improves as K increases.
quotes: It combined 12 two-qubit PQCs with a depth of 2, allowing the approximation of a degree-4 polynomial through a combination of lower-degree ones.
Additionally, Taylor coefficients were stored in a separate matrix of size K2 × 12.
The number of trainable parameters varied from 120 (K = 2) to 1272 (K = 10), each initialized randomly from [0, π].
The achieved MSE on the test data was 2.22 × 10−4 (K = 2) and 9.82 × 10−5 (K = 10).
As K increases, the PQC demonstrates improved approximation performance, aligning with the theoretical findings.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study, two settings of K.
assertions.reader_inference: The stated counts fit 72 circuit parameters plus K squared times 12 coefficient entries (48 for K = 2, 1200 for K = 10), so most of the parameters at K = 10 are entries of the coefficient matrix. Only two values of K were run. The experiment is a proof of principle that trains this structure, not a run of the LCU and Hadamard-test construction of Theorem 4.

assertions.value: The authors state that for Lipschitz functions the global (Bernstein) approach reaches error 2ε with n = (2ddℓ2)/ε3 and parameters of the printed order O 2d2 dd+1ℓ2d/ε3d, while the local approach reaches error 2ε with K = d/ε and parameters of the printed order O dd/2/εd, and conclude that the local approach is better; the local analysis sets β = 1, thus s = 0 in Theorem 4.
quotes: By selecting n = (2ddℓ2)/ε3, we ensure an approximation error of 2ε.
Setting K = d/ε ensures a 2ε approximation error, with the number of trainable parameters scaling as O dd/2/εd
we set β = 1, thus s = 0 in Theorem 4, in accordance with the Lipschitz continuous property exhibited by the target function.
assertions.certainty_reason: Derived by the authors from Theorems 3 and 4; the s = 0 case is outside Theorem 4's stated hypothesis.
assertions.reader_inference: Theorem 4 requires s to be a positive integer; this comparison uses s = 0. With s = 0 the 'Taylor expansion' is the constant f(eta/K), so the local bound is a piecewise-constant bound of order root-d over K.

assertions.value: The authors state that they gauge model size by the product of width and depth, that for error ε the PQC size scales as O(K_Q to the power d times d to the power (s + 1)) and the near-optimal ReLU network size as O(K_C to the power (d over 2) times s to the power (d + 3)), with K_Q = Θ(d2/ε1/s) and K_C = Θ(sd/s/ε1/s).
quotes: Here, we use a straightforward measure, the product of width and depth, to gauge the model size.
By setting approximation error as ε, the size of PQC and FNN scale as O(KQd ds+1) and O(KCd/2sd+3), respectively, where KQ = Θ(d2/ε1/s) and KC = Θ(sd/s/ε1/s).
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' substitution into upper bounds of two constructions.
assertions.reader_inference: Both sides are upper bounds. The product of width and depth ignores the shots needed to read the PQC output.

assertions.value: The authors state that for error ε the number of trainable parameters of the PQC scales as O(K_Q to the power d times d to the power (s + 1)) and that of the ReLU network as O(K_C to the power ((1+λ0)d/2) times s to the power (2d + 4)), with λ0 in (0, 1) the ReLU width hyperparameter, and that for 2 ≤ s < d the ratio is of the printed order, so the PQC parameter count is significantly lower.
quotes: By setting approximation error as ε, the number of trainable parameters of PQC and FNN scale as O(KQd ds+1) and O(KC(1+λ0)d/2s2d+4), respectively.
Here, the hyperparameter λ0 ∈ (0, 1) signifies FNN’s width.
assertions.certainty_reason: A comparison of upper bounds by the authors.

assertions.value: The authors state that PQCs capture monomial functions of degree s exactly, so no approximation is needed, whereas the ReLU networks approximate them with error shown in Table S1, and conclude PQCs are promising candidates for outperforming FNNs on more complex target spaces.
assertions.anchor: Appendix E, p.32; Table S1, p.31
quotes: Notably, PQCs possess the unique capability to capture the dynamics of monomial functions precisely, eliminating the need for approximation and thereby offering a compelling advantage.
These advantages position PQCs as promising candidates for outperforming FNNs when addressing more complex target function spaces.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim; the exactness is of the expectation value (Lemma S5).
assertions.reader_inference: The exactness holds for the exact expectation value of a monomial whose absolute value is at most 1 and for a PQC with a free angle choice that the authors give by existence; it does not include sampling error.

assertions.value: The authors state that all variables in their PQCs are parameters of single-qubit rotation gates, with no classical parameterized pre- or post-processing, so it is not ambiguous whether the expressivity comes from the classical or the quantum part, and that the constructions rely on no impractical assumptions.
assertions.anchor: Section 1, p.2; Section 5, p.9; Appendix A.3, p.20
quotes: This eliminates the ambiguity regarding whether the expressivity originates from classical or quantum parts.
All the variables take the form of parameters within single-qubit rotation gates, avoiding any classical parameterized pre-processing or post-processing.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim about their own construction.
assertions.reader_inference: The localization step and the grid index come from a floor applied to an expectation value, and the Taylor coefficients are classical numbers from the target's derivatives (Lemma S15); neither is parameterized pre-processing in the paper's sense, but the first is a classical step between two circuits.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing Zhao et al., that exponential lower bounds on the number of trainable parameters in terms of the number of variables were proved for approximating bounded Lipschitz continuous functions with PQCs without parameterized classical data processing, so PQCs still suffer the curse of dimensionality for Lipschitz functions, and that this does not rule out the same rate with smaller PQCs than classical networks.
quotes: proved exponential lower bounds on the number of trainable parameters (in terms of the number of variables) needed for approximating bounded Lipschitz continuous functions using PQCs without parameterized classical data processing
However, this does not rule out the possibility that one can achieve the same approximation rate with PQCs of smaller size compared to classical deep neural networks.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result attributed to [42].
assertions.reader_inference: The paper's own PQC sizes have a K to the d factor, consistent with exponential growth in d.

assertions.value: The authors state that their results are, to the best of their knowledge, the first explicit PQC constructions for approximating Lipschitz continuous and Hölder smooth functions with quantitative approximation error bounds.
quotes: To the best of our knowledge, our results establish the first explicit PQC constructions for approximating Lipschitz continuous and Hölder smooth functions with quantitative approximation error bounds.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author priority claim.

assertions.value: The authors state that by comparison with the near-optimal approximation bound for classical ReLU networks they demonstrate an improvement over classical models on approximating high-dimensional functions satisfying specific smoothness criteria, in model size and number of parameters.
quotes: we demonstrate an improvement over the classical models on approximating high-dimensional functions that satisfy specific smoothness criteria, quantified by an improvement on the model size and the number of parameters.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author conclusion resting on a comparison of upper bounds.
assertions.reader_inference: No lower bound on the classical side and no sampling cost on the quantum side is stated; see pqc-vs-relu-size.

assertions.value: The authors state as future work exploring more powerful PQC constructions, understanding capabilities and limitations of PQCs in practical tasks even with real-world data, and developing efficient training strategies, such as faster-converging methods; they introduce the nested PQC structure as novel.
quotes: Future work could focus on exploring more powerful PQC constructions based on our proposed idea and understanding the capabilities and limitations of PQCs in more practical tasks even with real-world data.
Developing efficient training strategies for PQCs, such as accelerated methods that achieve faster convergence rates, will also be interesting.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' own list of open problems (Section 5).
assertions.reader_inference: The theorems construct circuits by existence; trainability of the constructed angles is not addressed.
